Acorn protesters force council meeting to be abandoned after anger over bailiffs The community union is calling on the council to stop sending bailiffs Alex Seabrook Local democracy reporter Furious protesters angry at the city council’s use of bailiffs sparked chaos at City Hall last night. The Bristol City Council meeting was eventually abandoned and the police called. Members of the community union Acorn began shouting about bailiffs, leading the lord mayor to pause the meeting and then later postpone the rest of the agenda. Acorn is calling on the council to protect “vulnerable residents” with unpaid council tax debts from bailiffs turning up at their homes. Councillors decamped to the Conference Hall next to the main chamber, as security guards blocked protesters from entering through the doors. The meeting last night (Nov 10), was hearing an update about how the recent schools hack had affected children. But then Green Councillor Tony Dyer, leader of the council, was interrupted by Acorn members. A debate on social care cuts was scrapped too. An Acorn spokesperson said: “We’ve spent more than a year campaigning, meeting councillors and putting evidence in front of the council. We secured a significant commitment from the leader, and we expected that commitment to mean something. We were told vulnerable residents who couldn’t afford to pay would be protected from bailiffs. “But after months of discussions, the proposals we’ve now been shown don’t deliver what was promised. People struggling with debt need protection they can rely on, not another round of assurances. Our members have voted to take action, and that’s why we’re here tonight. Bristol City Council needs to honour its promises.” Acorn’s campaign has been supported by 39 councillors, over half the 70 councillors in Bristol, with an open letter calling on Cllr Dyer to end bailiff enforcement for council debt against residents receiving council tax support or benefits, or working on low incomes. The union said new proposed protections for people in debt are weaker than commitments made last year. The previous week Acorn members gathered outside City Hall on Bonfire Night and symbolically burned bills. Around 25 members disrupted the full council meeting, with some in the public gallery and the rest in the foyer of City Hall. When the police arrived the protest remained peaceful as officers spoke with Acorn members and council staff. After a long discussion, the lord mayor and some councillors returned to the council chamber, and the meeting was adjourned. The rest of the agenda will likely be discussed next month instead. Similar disruptions in City Hall have happened before, including in 2023 when the police were called, when Barton House tenants confronted the former mayor Marvin Rees. According to Acorn, the latest proposed protections from the council are limited to people who are on the council tax reduction scheme. Around 31,500 households in Bristol get either a full or partial discount on council tax, of which 21,500 are working age and the rest pensioners. This scheme is the only mechanism the council has to identify low-income households, according to a council source. There could be the potential to go further on ending the use of bailiffs, but this could mean the council losing a lot of money which would then impact public services. Acorn has been campaigning for two years to change the council’s policy on bailiffs, after figures showed a huge increase since the pandemic, with 27,000 sent in one year alone. Last year, Cllr Dyer appeared to promise an end to their use for vulnerable people, and those on benefits or low incomes, but then clarified the following month that bailiffs would still be used to collect council tax debt. The council leader has now said that new proposals have been worked up by a cross-party group of councillors, which will be considered by a policy committee next month. He added that council tax funds services like rubbish collection and education. In a statement, Cllr Dyer said: “Every local authority has a legal responsibility to collect council tax and it funds vital local services such as social care, education, and waste management. We remain determined to balance this legal responsibility with a compassionate approach that recognises and supports residents facing financial challenges. The use of enforcement agents to collect any council debt is always a last resort. “It is our priority to work with vulnerable residents and those who are in receipt of council tax reduction to encourage open conversations about their individual circumstances and wherever possible help with additional support so that they can pay their council tax. “Proposals for how we can best manage our approach for collecting council tax debt from those in receipt of council tax reduction have been developed by a cross-party task and finish group dedicated to improving support for low-income households.” The council leader added: “The deputy leader and lead officers have met with various agencies and representative groups to fashion these proposals, including regular meetings with Acorn to discuss their campaign aims. These proposals are currently due to be considered by Strategy and Resources Committee on December 14. “We continue to urge residents who have concerns about their ability to pay their council tax bill to contact us as soon as possible so that we can work together to find the best solution.”

stories.text: ‘Thatcher’s Greatest Blunder’ article about Poll Tax, by Michael Crick and Adrian Van Klaveren. For a complete account of how Mrs Thatcher and her party came to adopt the poll tax we will have to wait until the public records become available around 2015. Even then we may not get the full history. In December 1990 BBC ‘Panorama’ began piecing together an interim version of the story, attempting to trace the true origins of the poll tax, and to ascertain exactly who deserves responsibility or blame. Eventually our research was overtaken by the Gulf War, and it will never be used for a ‘Panorama’ programme. But it is still worth placing some of our work on record. Most of those who helped devise the poll tax went on to greater glory. Christopher Foster was knighted in 1986; Terence Heiser got his knighthood the following year having been made DoE Permanent Secretary in 1985; Peter Owen became a Deputy Secretary in the Department; Anthony Mayer went to work for Lord Rothschild at his bank before being appointed chief executive at the Housing Corporation in 1991; Jill Rutter returned to the Treasury and served for a year as private secretary to an up-and-coming Chief Secretary, John Major; Roger Bright stayed in the DoE and was perhaps ideally qualified to take charge of Michael Heseltine’s enquiry into the poll tax in the winter of 1990–91; Oliver Letwin is the Conservative candidate for Hampstead and Highgate, a marginal seat where his Labour opponent Glenda Jackson has tried to make much political capital of his role in inventing the poll tax. But the two ministers who actually devised and recommended the poll tax, William Waldegrave and Kenneth Baker, suffered few recriminations, and were both rewarded by Mrs Thatcher with prominent jobs in Cabinet. Both men have had their political difficulties in the last year – Waldegrave over the health reforms, and Baker over the Brixton prison escape – but on the blunder these two former Heathites were most responsible for” they somehow managed to escape almost unharmed.

UK profits of energy firms exceed £143bn in 6 years as public braces for bills hike A tally of profit announcements from 33 energy firms has revealed the vast sums being made as households suffer a sixth winter of high energy bills. Over £143 billion of UK profits have been generated since 2020 and since the start of 2026, the End Fuel Poverty Coalition has tracked over £10 billion in UK profits reported by the firms as gas prices have surged. [1] Globally, the profits of the 33 firms since 2020 stand in excess of half a trillion pounds with £152 billion being made in 2026 alone. Included in the totals are profits from BP that posted £13bn in global profits for the first 9 months of 2026 and who attributed much of its results to market trading business units that buy, sell and move energy around the world. Trading is a key part of the global system which is keeping gas and oil prices high for consumers in the UK. Gas prices have stood at record highs on wholesale markets in recent weeks, with a fresh spike occurring at the time that Ofgem are monitoring prices to set the price cap that comes into force on 1 January. Current predictions are that the average energy bill will increase by 26% from today’s prices as increases to the cost households pay for gas have surged by 267% since January 2021, ahead of inflation and wages. [2] According to polling by Survation, 59% of the public believe the level of profits that have been made by the energy industry since 2020 are unacceptable as over two thirds (67%) of UK adults said they were worried about paying their energy bills if prices rise again in the new year. Figures show that since 2023, a third of the public have cut back on energy use in part due to the cost and that 22% of adults are worried about falling behind on their energy bills. But as households suffer, analysis of the value of bosses’ shareholdings shows that the heads of 12 firms including BP, Equinor and Shell have together seen the value of their personal stakes in their firms rise by a combined £120 million between 26 February and 30 October 2026. [3] Updated analysis of the publicly declared interests of members of the House of Lords shows that just a dozen members of the upper house sit on shares worth almost £2m, an increase of £475,000 in 2026 alone. Simon Francis, coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, commented: “From the North Sea fossil fuel firms to the energy network operators in Cornwall, huge profits have consistently been posted by the energy industry in Britain while the public suffer from high bills. “This is now the sixth winter where energy prices have been well ahead of long-term norms and the reality is that the cost of gas, which is driving the crisis, has been out pacing inflation and wage earnings. “It’s no wonder that households are struggling to keep up and many are falling behind with their bills. “As well as a long term plan to get the country off gas and heating oil for good, households also need help now. With the next price cap announcement looming, time is running out for Ministers to implement more support for people this winter.”…

It is a new approach to government, judging all policies through the lens of our least well-off communities and whether they will make life better there or worse. stories.text: Steve Wright on Britain’s economic decline since Britain joined EEC in 1973. Corbyn and Brexit. Burnham at the Guildhall: Now, I know it would be much easier to say nothing about the EU. That’s probably the conventional Westminster view. But if we are [music] going to be serious about growth, then we are going to have to have this conversation. And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain. Well, we’re now joined by Steve Wright, who’s the founder of Britain Unbound. Steve, good morning. Thank you for joining us in the studio. What are your feelings about stirring the Brexit pot again? Well, I I’m not really relishing the idea of having to fight the battle again for another decade, which is what will end up happening. This isn’t something that happens very quickly. We can see through the the decades of history with the EU that these things never move quickly. And so the idea of of having to fight that battle on a daily basis is is quite daunting, but something that I imagine we will win yet again and with a higher percentage. And the prime minister is talking about if if we’re going to be serious about growth. I don’t recall stellar growth for this economy when we were in the European Union. No, not at all. If you look at the the figures for UK GDP growth uh before and after we joined the EEC, then it it takes a massive nose dive afterwards. And so if anything, the evidence suggests that that really the growth is for for innovative economies that are sitting outside of bureaucratic laws that that even other EU member states are now saying there have been too many of in the last few years and they need to slow down and stop making laws because it’s impacting their economy. What do you make of Burnham’s phrase that Britain has been diminished in the eyes of the world because of Brexit? Do you think we have lost some soft power with some countries? I I think that um we’ve reached out to the rest of the world. We’ve reached out to the Commonwealth. We’ve reached out to the Anglosphere. Uh and and actually we have trade deals now that we would never have had and and and deals. You look at the Orcus Agreement. You look at uh the trade deals with the Gulf uh Gulf Cooperation Council, with the CPTP, with with the with India, those wouldn’t have existed if we hadn’t left the EU. And so actually when you look at what the UK has done in in such a short amount of time really what we’ve done is reach out to the rest of the world not go insular. What if I mean immigration was a big factor in the referendum campaign. We know he’s going to sign up to to much closer integration on Friday. How do you fight back this time? Well, the the difficulty is there’s a number of narratives that have been that have been spun and I can understand why they’ve been spun, but but it is a narrative all the same. And and one is the fact that um we we lost control of our borders after we left the EU. We haven’t lost the control of the borders. We’ve just refused to actually enforce the borders that we now have control of. And actually um the the the electorate punished the Conservative government by removing them because they didn’t do what they had the power to be able to do. So we have that power. We’re just not utilizing it as well as we should do. Well, what power have we got that they’re not we’re not using? It it is completely within our remit now is it’s our rule book. We can set the laws on on how many u migrants we allow into the country each year. And the the majority of the country have been screaming out for decades that they do understand that immigration is required. They do understand that that we need a certain amount of it, but for it to be controlled and for us to be able to choose uh who who joins the country and and if the current government, whoever whichever color that would be, would be to implement that policy and to have more control of the borders, then they would find themselves very popular with the electorate.

Genealogy of a Controversy: Development of an Anti-Fertility Vaccine The history of the development of a new scientific or medical technology is a story of science in the making. In this paper we attempt to trace the development of the anti-hCG vaccine over the past 20 years, using controversy as a methodological entry point into the history. The anti-hCG vaccine is one of the range of immunological contraceptives that is being researched and developed in laboratories around the world. There are two teams which have been working on this research since the early 1970s – Talwar and his team at the NII in India, and Stevens at the University of Ohio.1 Both the vaccines have gone in for phase I trials and Talwar’s vaccine has also completed phase II clinical trials. For one thing, it should prove possible to develop vaccines that are unlikely to disrupt the menstrual cycle or cause the side-effects associated with hormonal contraceptives. Fertility-regulating vaccines should be well accepted by users, given the general popularity of immunization. stories.text: NY Times – Elon Musk on civilian Starlink and military Starshield – Zelensky lies. Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield restrictions in Ukraine SpaceX founder Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of lying about speed limits affecting Ukraine’s Starshield network. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that those restrictions are still in place. Musk said that Starlink is speed-limited because it is not intended for offensive operations, which he said must instead use Starshield. founder Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being untruthful about restrictions around Ukraine’s Starshield network and said Kyiv wanted to use Starlink for offensive operations. Asked at The New York Times’ Dealbook Summit about Zelenskyy’s claims that Starshield had been slowed down, Musk said, “That’s false … I don’t want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful.” When pressed on whether he meant Ukraine was not always truthful, Musk doubled down with a reply: “No, it’s not always truthful.” His comments came after Zelenskyy on Wednesday said speed restrictions remained in place on Starshield, hampering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missile and drone strikes. “We are discussing this with the American side,” he said. Ukraine relies heavily on SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield for capabilities like battlefield communications and drone operations. Musk has previously said that “if we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately.” The SpaceX CEO sought to distinguish between Starlink, a commercial satellite network, and Starshield, a military system developed by SpaceX and operated by the U.S. government. Musk said that Starlink is subject to speed limits because it is not intended for offensive military operations, adding that such missions should instead use the Starshield network. “Any action taken by Starshield is up to the War Department. Starlink is commercial and is not intended as a weapon of war,” Musk said, referring to the U.S. Department of Defense. In October, Musk said the U.S. government and President Donald Trump were responsible for any restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield network after slowdowns to the service were reported. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X. The Wall Street Journal later reported on Oct. 20 that Musk had ordered the slowdown, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter. “What I’m trying to tell you is Zelenskyy is actually asking to use the Starlink commercial satellites for events of military actions, and we have declined to do so, as we have declined to do so from the beginning of this conflict,” Musk added in the interview. On Oct. 24, Musk said SpaceX had restricted Ukraine’s access to Starlink because Kyiv had violated the service’s terms by using it for offensive drone strikes, a claim Ukrainian officials disputed. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk wrote on X one day after. CNBC has reached out to Ukraine’s ministry of foreign affairs for comment but did not receive a response. The president’s office could not immediately be reached.

SHAEF Intelligence Report EW-Pa 128 (AKA the “Red House Report”): Real Plan or Red Herring? June 3, 2025 by NationalArchivesBlog, posted in State and Foreign Affairs, World War II Download the cover despatch and the entire report here. There is no document in the National Archives entitled the “Red House Report.” There is, however, a SHAEF intelligence report that mentions a late 1944 meeting that took place at the Hotel Rotes Haus [Red House] in Strasbourg, France, that has become known colloquially as the “Red House Report.” On November 7, 1944, the SHAEF G-2 Economic Section prepared a 3-page report on a meeting of German industrialists and military officials in the Hotel Rotes Haus in Strasbourg, France. In that meeting they discussed plans for engaging “in underground activity after Germany’s defeat” and the transfer of funds to neutral countries. The report was numbered EW-Pa 128. Twenty days later, on November 27, the Economic Warfare Division of the U.S. embassy in London sent a typescript copy of the report to the Department of State as one of its “Economic Warfare (Safehaven) Series” of reports for use by the Department of State, the Department of the Treasury, and the Foreign Economic Administration (FEA). The Department of State further distributed copies of the despatch and its enclosure to several other agencies and U.S. embassies overseas. The despatch and its enclosure, both as clear and bright today as the day they were typed, were indexed to the Department of State’s central files with the file designation for the general file on monetary system, coinage, currency, and mint (“800.515”). Markings on the document indicate that it was declassified no later than 1991 but more likely in the early 1970s. “Safehaven” refers to the program established in late 1944, after it became clear that the Germans were attempting to move assets abroad in the face of imminent defeat. The aim of the program was to collect information about “enemy investments and plans, and the activities of persons which could be employed as a means of preserving the enemy’s economic, political and military potential abroad after the cessation of hostilities.” On December 1, 1944, the Economic Intelligence Officer of the Economic Warfare Division in the U.S. embassy in London sent another copy of the SHAEF report to the Department of State along with copies for the G-2 Section in the War Department and the Economic Warfare Division of the Department of Justice as one of its “Economic Warfare (Intelligence) Series” of reports. The embassy made direct distribution to the Foreign Economic Administration (FEA), the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) offices in Washington and London, the U.S. Control Commission, and the European Advisory Committee and the Department distributed copies of the despatch and its enclosure to several other agencies. This copy was a printed and included a pre-printed cover note attached to other reports, too, that indicated the report had “been duplicated and given wider circulation because its contents are believed significant and of general interest to agencies concerned with the post-hostilities situation in Europe.” The dispatch with its enclosure, still bright and clear, was placed in the Department of State central files with the file number for the economic warfare intelligence reports from the embassy in London (“740.00112 Intelligence”). This document was declassified in 1972….

They lied to us for 25 years about the 9/11 attacks – Russell Brand Twenty-five years after 9/11, some of the most uncomfortable questions surrounding that day still refuse to disappear. From the collapse of Building 7 and the wars that followed to Jon Stewart highlighting newly released records showing authorities knew about toxic air around Ground Zero, Russell asks why citizens should simply trust institutions that have repeatedly concealed information—and who really benefits when a crisis becomes an opportunity for greater power and control. The Federal Emergency Management Agency reported that the collapse was due primarily to fire, but what does it look like to you? Seems like a leading question, but I suppose are we supposed to say controlled demolition? And if all of those girders simultaneously imploded, the indication is that they were simultaneously sabotaged or impacted. I’m seeing some people that I happen to know work loosely in the field of construction nodding their heads, but I won’t turn the cameras to them just now in case their jobs require that they don’t say things like your own government performed a terrorist act against you in order to introduce the Patriot Act and to delegitimize a series of foreign wars, the consequences of which we’re all experiencing. As I tell you frequently when I fly through Atlanta airport, I am informed that every day they receive the coffins of service personnel. Every day it’s just normal for them to receive the dead bodies of brave Americans who are dying for one would have to say, well, I don’t know. You tell me whether you believe their lives are being wisely spent. Questions you’re not allowed to ask. Why did the owner of the World Trade Center get maximum insurance against terrorist attacks 6 weeks prior to September 11th? Why did the owner have breakfast in the towers every morning except for September 11th? The day before September 11th, Rumsfeld gave a press conference where he talked about trillions of dollars missing. Our financial systems are decades old. According to some estimates, we cannot track $2.3 trillion in transactions. Why was CNN already there before the attacks with a camera crew ready to film? Why was there an unidentified group of short cells purchased against airline companies right before the attacks? Why was every [music] passenger incinerated in the explosion, but the terrorist passport somehow survived? Why was a report published a year before 911 by George W. Bush’s administration saying they needed to aggressively expand military power worldwide, but they need a catalyzing Pearl Harbor level event in order to gain public support? Certainly a lot to contemplate there.

stories.text: WHAT’S NVIDIA SCANDAL REALLY ABOUT 1? OPEN VS. CLOSED SOURCE: Jensen Wong, Nvidia, resigns after affair with alleged Chinese spy lady. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source, whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

stories.subtitle: Maybe they had a point, as various technologies are hacked or go wrong, and go down. Chinese workers on strike as robots take over.
stories.text: The Luddites. Maybe they had a point, as various technologies are hacked or go wrong, and go down. Chinese workers on strike as robots take over. Digital Luddites are rising. They want to democratise tech, not destroy it Have you ever been called a Luddite? We have – usually as an insult, rooted in a popular misconception that Luddites are anti-progress fanatics. Nothing could be further from the truth. The original 19th century Luddites weren’t against technology. Rather, they resisted its oppressive use. Their rebellion was violently suppressed. But their core critique lives on: technology should benefit all of humanity, not a privileged few. Today, as Silicon Valley billionaires and United States president Donald Trump turbocharge corporate control of public digital infrastructure, this critique rings truer than ever. In response, we are a seeing a growing surge of attempts to wrest back control of technology for democratic ends. This is a kind of “digital Luddism” which echoes past struggles against high-tech injustice. The original Luddites The Luddites were 19th century English textile workers who destroyed machinery threatening their craft and livelihoods. Historians call their tactics “collective bargaining by riot”. They were fighting against technologies that centralised power and stripped workers of dignity. Luddite resistance was part of broader struggles for labour rights and socioeconomic justice. For example, in 18th century France, silk weavers similarly revolted against mechanisation that devalued their craft. Earlier, England’s Diggers and Levellers resisted the privatisation of communal lands. This foreshadowed today’s battles over corporate control of digital infrastructure. The Luddites faced severe punishment, including imprisonment and even execution. Despite this, their legacy endures. Today, dismissing critics of Big Tech as “Luddites” repeats the mistake of conflating resistance to exploitation with fear of progress. The Luddite resistance in the 19th century was part of broader struggles for labour rights and socioeconomic justice. Working Class Movement Library catalogue In the most extreme scenario, unchecked corporate power allied with monstrous government polices can lead to atrocities. In Nazi Germany, for example, Dehomag, a former subsidiary of computer giant IBM, provided data systems to the Nazis to track victims. Chemical company IG Farben also supplied Zyklon B gas for extermination camps. Many other companies profited from forced labour and funded the regime. This shows how complicity can make oppression more efficient. Today, digital technologies are deepening inequality, eroding democracy, undermining privacy, and concentrating power. Digital technologies are also fuelling surveillance capitalism, the displacement of human workers by AI algorithms and the growth of monopolistic platforms. Platforms and AI systems governed by “broligarchs” such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg are also shaping politics, culture, and beliefs globally. Digital Luddism, also known as neo-Luddism, tackles these issues through three strategies: resistance, removal and replacement. Resistance: blocking harmful systems Technology is not inevitable — it’s a choice. Sustained collective action can counter corporate dominance and align tech with democratic values. In 2018, more than 3,000 Google workers protested the company’s military AI contract, forcing it to adopt ethical guidelines. However, in February this year, Google expanded defence deals, showing how resistance must be sustained. Three years later, Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen exposed the harmful algorithms at the heart of the social media platform. Then, in 2024, Amazon and Google staff also staged walkouts over a US$1.2 billion AI contract linked to Israeli military operations. Creative industries are also fighting back. For example, in 2023 screenwriters and actors in Hollywood protested against AI replacing their roles. Similarly, Australia’s “right to disconnect” law reflects Luddite principles of reclaiming autonomy. Non-profit organisations such as the Algorithmic Justice League and the Electronic Frontier Foundation empower digital rights advocates to take back control over digital spaces by exposing AI bias and through legal litigation.

Iran state TV says new Khorramshahr missile could reach US base in Britain Iranian state television has warned that modified versions of the country’s Khorramshahr ballistic missile could reach American military bases in Europe, explicitly naming RAF Fairford in Britain as a potential target. “The range of Iran’s missiles is not limited to what they have seen,” the report, broadcast Saturday, said, claiming that modifications to the Khorramshahr’s warhead could increase its range severalfold. The Khorramshahr-4, unveiled in 2023, has a claimed range of 2,000 kilometers while carrying a warhead weighing 1,500 kilograms. A lighter warhead could extend its range, although the extent of any increase remains unverified. The broadcast included a review of missiles and drones Iran has used in its wars with Israel and the United States since June 2025, presenting the Khorramshahr as part of a broader arsenal capable of threatening American installations farther afield. In a warning directed at Britain, the report suggested that British air defenses were not necessarily more capable than Israel’s, which it claimed Iranian missiles had already penetrated during the war. There has been no independent confirmation that Iran possesses a modified Khorramshahr capable of reaching RAF Fairford. The broadcast invoked an order by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that Iran’s armed forces should face no geographical restrictions in responding to attacks by the United States or Israel. Khamenei issued the directive on October 31, calling for immediate and effective retaliation without geographical limits and ordering military commanders to update their list of potential targets. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards subsequently said the country’s longstanding self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometers on ballistic missile ranges had been lifted, although they did not specify whether longer-range missiles had been developed or deployed. The broadcast follows a series of warnings from senior Iranian officials that American bases in Europe and on distant islands could become targets if Washington launches further attacks. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said earlier this week that Tehran would no longer confine its response to nearby US military installations and could strike bases in European countries. The threats come as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Tehran demanding an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and relief from sanctions before negotiations can resume. Washington has maintained its economic pressure campaign, while President Donald Trump has declared that he wants a total victory over Iran and suggested the United States no longer needs a negotiated agreement. The latest state television report went further than previous warnings by naming a specific British installation and linking the threat to a purportedly extended-range version of the Khorramshahr missile.

stories.text: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased. LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an air base in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran. A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased. They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. The official would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped-up security. At least eight air refueling tankers and three Osprey tilt-rotor aircraft left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed. Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to air bases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk. It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain, RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terrorist plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike Iran. The Wall Street Journal, which was first to report on this week’s movements, said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said that the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and that it remained under discussion by U.S. officials. “We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News. A U.S. European Command official said: “U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement. U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.” A spokesperson for the U.K. Defense Ministry said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.” “Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said. The U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford last month following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials have told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at the base, which is in Gloucestershire.

UK must be ready to fight war in three years, says Army head Britain must be ready to fight a war in three years, the new head of the Army has said. Gen Sir Roland ‘Rolly-Poley’ Walker has warned against a range of threats in what he called an “increasingly volatile” world. But he said war was not inevitable and the Army had “just enough time” to prepare itself to avoid conflict . Central to this was doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and tripling it by the end of the decade, he said. In his first speech in the role on Tuesday, Gen Walker said the UK faced danger from an “axis of upheaval”. Among the key threats facing the UK in the coming years, highlighted by the general in a briefing, is an angered Russia, which could seek retribution against the West for supporting Ukraine, regardless of who wins the war. He said: “It doesn’t matter how it ends. I think Russia will emerge from it probably weaker objectively – or absolutely – but still very, very dangerous and wanting some form of retribution for what we have done to help Ukraine.” He also warned that China was intent on retaking Taiwan, and Iran was likely to pursue nuclear weapons. He said the threats they posed could become particularly acute within the next three years, and that since the war in Ukraine these countries had created a “mutual transactional relationship”, sharing weapons and technology. But he said the path to war was not “inexorable” if the UK re-established credible land forces to support its strategy of deterrence to avoid war. He did not directly appeal for further funding or troops in his speech, describing his force of just over 70,000 regular troops as a “medium-sized army”. But he urged the British Army to modernise quickly – including focusing on technology like Artificial Intelligence and firepower, rather than numbers. Eventually, his ambition is for the Army to be able to destroy an enemy three times its own size. This would mean firing faster and further, he said, helped by learning the lessons from the war in Ukraine…

Anti-Zionism: A revelatory Jewish history from the Pulitzer Prize winner by Benjamin Moser (2026) ‘Astonishing … A work of moral courage’ BRIAN ENO ‘Affecting … beautifully written’ GUARDIAN ‘Remarkable’ YANIS VAROUFAKIS A sweeping and revelatory history of the hidden tradition of Jewish thinkers who opposed Zionism from Pulitzer Prize winner Benjamin Moser. In Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History, Benjamin Moser uncovers a suppressed tradition that has shaped Jewish thought for generations. Through a cast of artists, rabbis, poets, lawyers, activists, journalists and politicians – across Europe, North American, Africa, Asia and Latin America – Moser traces a lineage of Jewish dissenters who confronted Zionism’s moral and political stakes – often at devastating personal cost, including censorship, exile and death. Their lives form a sweeping, global narrative that dismantles a powerful myth: that anti-Zionism is synonymous with antisemitism. Spanning continents and centuries, these voices – people from the right and the left, Reform and Orthodox, Ashkenazic and Sephardic, men and women, gay and straight – differ sharply in belief and background, yet converge on a shared warning about the consequences of a nationalist project built on exclusion. What emerges is not only a rediscovered tradition of Jewish moral thought, but a startling reappraisal of Zionism itself. Moser’s work restores the full scale and depth of Jewish ethical imagination, affirming that Judaism is older and larger than any single political project. Lucid, rigorous and deeply humane, Anti-Zionism cements Moser’s place as one of our foremost Jewish thinkers and presents a framework through which this history – and its meanings – will be understood for years to come. ‘An urgent rebuke to Likud’s dangerous rewriting of history’ AFUA HIRSCH, author of Decolonising My Body ‘Brave and passionate … An important and revelatory contribution to the growing debate on the ethics of Zionism’ WILLIAM DALRYMPLE, author of The Golden Road ‘Finally we have a way to understand the best parts of Jewish history’ NAN GOLDIN ‘A necessary book that carries its passions with the urgent clarity and moral grace that its subject and the moment deserve’ HISHAM MATAR, author of The Return ‘Anti-Zionism restores our faith in what Iris Murdoch defined as the Sovereignty of Good’ YANIS VAROUFAKIS, author of Technofeudalism ‘What I learned in these pages has profoundly changed my understanding of history – the world’s, my people’s, my family’s, and my own’ AYELET WALDMAN, author of A Perfect Hand ‘An urgently necessary refutation … I hope it will be widely read’ PETER SINGER, author of The Life You Can Save

stories.text: Plan to integrate US and Israel military. Twelve Senators Call for US-Israel Military Integration To Be Removed from NDAA The letter, led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, also calls for the removal of an amendment that would mandate an increase in US intelligence sharing to Israel A group of 12 senators has written to congressional leadership urging the removal of provisions from the House and Senate versions of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would mandate increased US-Israeli military and intelligence cooperation. The idea of the amendments is to further integrate the US and Israeli militaries and make the special relationship harder to unwind, a reaction to the increasing criticism of Israel among Americans. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing for the integration, which he has referred to as “my plan,” and says it will come with a phase-out of US financial military aid to Israel over time, but defense analysts have warned the aid will just be buried in the Pentagon budget and less visible to the public. While both the House and the Senate have included the integration plan in their draft NDAAs, the two chambers have yet to go to conference to negotiate the final bill, where the amendments could potentially be stripped out. The letter, led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and signed by nine other Democrats and one Independent (Sen. Bernie Sanders), urges congressional leaders to “exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the US-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining US interests and values.” The senators said that the “provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect US national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.” The letter calls for the removal of Section 219 from the House bill and Section 1217 from the Senate one, which both “mandate the creation of a ‘United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative’ to expand and accelerate the US-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development.” They said that the provisions would “threaten US national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology.” The letter also calls for the removal of Section 618 of the Senate’s Intelligence Authorization Act, which would mandate increased intelligence sharing with Israel. “The provision would tie the President’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect US national security. That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level,” the letter reads.

Andy Burnham commits to not reopening divisive debate over the European Union – Makerfield by-election campaign 18 May 2006 Burnham reignites Britain’s divisive Brexit debate with his push for closer EU ties Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reignited the Brexit debate by suggesting the U.K. should seek closer ties with the European Union, and even consider rejoining Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reignited the divisive Brexit debate by suggesting the United Kingdom should seek closer ties with the European Union, including the possibility of rejoining the bloc. Marking his 100th day in office on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, Burnham argues that Brexit has failed to deliver economic growth and effective migration control. For a decade, British governments have observed a cardinal rule: Don’t mention Brexit. In particular, don’t suggest that voters’ 2016 decision to leave the European Union should be reversed. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who marked his 100th day in office on Tuesday, has broken that code of silence and reignited a debate that bitterly divided the country. He says Brexit has been a failure and the U.K. should seek a much closer relationship with the EU, with options up to and including rejoining the 27-nation bloc. “I am positive about closer ties with Europe and I’m not hiding that,” Burnham told the Sunday Times. “I think it will add to British GDP. I think it will give us stronger control of migration. I want to make those arguments.” In recent interviews, Burnham has said the country should have an “evidence-based debate” about the consequences of Brexit. He gave the example of immigration. Supporters of Brexit argued that it would give the country control over its borders by ending the right of EU citizens to live and work in the U.K., and of British nationals to settle across the bloc. While Britain now sets its own immigration policy, Burnham said leaving the bloc had made it harder to control unauthorized migration because Britain has lost access to EU databases and agreements. “The truth of the matter is we’ve lost immigration control in the way that we once had,” Burnham told broadcaster ITV on Monday. Brexit brought economic and political pain Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy, but few politicians have wanted to reopen the painful debate. The decision of British voters, by 52% to 48%, to leave the bloc after four decades of membership was followed by years of U.K.-EU wrangling over divorce terms. Britain finally left the EU in 2020 with a bare-bones trade deal that erected new barriers to doing business with the bloc of 450 million people on the U.K.’s doorstep…

stories.text: Lords evidence, Dominic Cummings stuns peers with rant about Britain’s ‘duff’ political system Boris Johnson’s former top adviser re-emerges from obscurity to give abrasive performance before a House of Lords committee Britain has moved on from the rancorous days of Covid lockdowns and the chaotic UK government of the time, led by Boris Johnson. BBC: Dominic Cummings , it seems, has not. The arch Brexiteer Cummings was Johnson’s conflict-prone chief adviser in Downing Street for most of 2020. He now works as a consultant and occasional Substack author. Select Committees – Lords Constitution Committee with Dominic CummingsCoverage of the Lords Constitution committee on the UK’s constitutional safeguards with evidence from the former chief adviser to prime minister Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings, on Wednesday 14 October 2026. On Wednesday morning he also appeared in front of a House of Lords committee to opine on the functioning of the UK’s unwritten constitution and its arms of government. Cummings gave a typically abrasive performance, a throwback to the old days when he prowled Downing Street while lambasting civil servants and Westminster journalists. He stunned the peers listening on Wednesday in the wood-panelled surrounds of committee room one with a litany of rants about Britain’s “duff” system of “shitshows” and his belief that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is not the main enemy, before aiming a series of digs at his political foes, including former UK health secretary Matt Hancock. “Do you really want Hancock making decisions?” he asked, seconds after subtly referencing the former politician’s pandemic-era marital affair with one of his aides. The Lords constitution committee was holding an inquiry into the UK’s balance of powers and its constitutional safeguards. It invited Cummings in to speak as a long-time critic of the system. He arrived displaying his characteristic sartorial style, clad in a crumpled shirt with sleeves rolled up, crumpled green anorak and red baseball cap. He launched into a lament about the “fake charade” of the existing system, in which an independent civil service is meant to serve UK governments of all hues. Things were better before 19th-century reforms ushered in the modern civil service and, he suggested, ministers were truly accountable to the UK parliament “That is the system under which the British Empire grew and we took over the world. Why can’t we have that system back?” he said. Cummings said “elite talent” no longer wanted to work in government, while the UK’s cabinet office, he suggested, had become too powerful and was now setting policy. “If you’ve got duff people, then the institutions will be duff,” he said. “Great people have options. They’re not going to go and sit in stupid meetings with PowerPoint after PowerPoint with no one actually taking responsibility for anything.” He suggested that all the “great people” he had encouraged into the cabinet office in 2020 had since been “pushed out” or “left in disgust” to work in fields such as artificial intelligence. Government had been left with “the worst kind of HR people”. At one point he cupped his ears while being questioned by a peer. “I’m sorry, my ears don’t work so well,” said Cummings. The peer was trying to ask him if the felt the UK’s constitution was “under threat”.

stories.text: The Horrors Of Big Pharma 1 Antidepressants: Prescription For Murder, BBC Panorama (2017) Can Sertraline kill you and your friends and induce mass shootings? James Holmes 2012 shooting – Recent regulatory warnings about adverse behavioural effects of antidepressants in susceptible individuals have raised the profile of these issues with clinicians, patients, and the public. We review available clinical trial data on paroxetine and sertraline and pharmacovigilance studies of paroxetine and fluoxetine, and outline a series of medico-legal cases involving antidepressants and violence. Both clinical trial and pharmacovigilance data point to possible links between these drugs and violent behaviours. The legal cases outlined returned a variety of verdicts that may in part have stemmed from different judicial processes. Many jurisdictions appear not to have considered the possibility that a prescription drug may induce violence . The association of antidepressant treatment with aggression and violence reported here calls for more clinical trial and epidemiological data to be made available and for good clinical descriptions of the adverse outcomes of treatment. Legal systems are likely to continue to be faced with cases of violence associated with the use of psychotropic drugs, and it may fall to the courts to demand access to currently unavailable data. The problem is international and calls for an international response. In 1989, Joseph Wesbecker shot dead eight people and injured 12 others before killing himself at his place of work in Kentucky. Wesbecker had been taking the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant fluoxetine for four weeks before these homicides, and this led to a legal action against the makers of fluoxetine, Eli Lilly. The case was tried and settled in 1994, and as part of the settlement a number of pharmaceutical company documents about drug-induced activation were released into the public domain. Subsequent legal cases, some of which are outlined below, have further raised the possibility of a link between antidepressant use and violence. The issue of treatment-related activation has since then been considered primarily in terms of possible increases in the risk of suicide among a subgroup of patients who react adversely to treatment. This possibility has led regulatory authorities to warn doctors about the risk of suicide in the early stages of treatment, at times of changing dosage, and during the withdrawal phase of treatment. Some regulators, such as the Canadian regulators, have also referred to risks of treatment-induced activation leading to both self-harm and harm to others [2]. The United States labels for all antidepressants as of August 2004 note that “anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, aggressiveness, impulsivity, akathisia (psychomotor restlessness), hypomania, and mania have been reported in adult and pediatric patients being treated with antidepressants for major depressive disorder as well as for other indications, both psychiatric and nonpsychiatric”. Despite these developments, few data are available on the links between antidepressant usage and violence. We here offer new data, review the implications of these data, and summarise a series of medico-legal cases. This paper focuses on paroxetine primarily because we have access to more illustrative medico-legal case material for this drug than for other antidepressants. Secondly, the manufacturer, GlaxoSmithKline, submitted data on the rates of occurrence of “hostile” episodes on paroxetine for the recent review of antidepressant drugs undertaken by the British regulator. It is not clear that the review team obtained comparable data for other antidepressants. The data submitted by GlaxoSmithKline on paroxetine for review by the Committee on Safety of Medicines Expert Working Group are described as a complete set of data from all placebo-controlled trials of this drug. The use of this dataset thus involves no selection by the authors, and any selection bias there might have been on the part of the company seems unlikely to have increased the size of the problem. Data from placebo-controlled trials of sertraline in children are also presented, as these also offer a complete dataset, so minimising any selection bias. E-mails from 1,374 patients in response to a BBC programme on paroxetine broadcast in 2002. One of us (AH) had the opportunity to analyse a complete set of these responses. In paroxetine clinical trials, aggression and violence were commonly coded under the rubric of hostility. This coding term includes homicide, homicidal acts, and homicidal ideation as well as aggressive events and “conduct disorders”, but no homicides were reported from these trials. The material posted on the company Web site suggests that these hostile behaviours in children primarily involved aggression rather than frank violence. When hostile events occurring in both adult and paediatric trials are summed, both on therapy and during the 30-day drug-free phase after taper had finished, 60 (0.65%) of 9,219 patients overall had hostile events. The tragic end of Gonzalo Lira: A voice silenced in Ukraine 13 January 2024 Gonzalo Lira, a Chilean-American war commentator known for his critical views on the Zelensky regime and Russia-Ukraine conflict, passed away on January 11, 2024, in a hospital in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Lira’s death followed an eight-month imprisonment on charges of ”justifying Russia’s military actions in Ukraine”, sparking international controversy and raising questions about freedom of speech and human rights during wartime. Gonzalo Lira gained notoriety in 2022 as a vocal critic of what he perceived as increasing authoritarianism in Ukraine. Lira saw the conflict as a proxy war waged by US against Russia and critisised the loss of life for a futile and unwindable war. His arrest in May 2023, under the charges of “production and dissemination of materials justifying Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine,” was a turning point. It not only highlighted the complexities of war-time free speech but also catalysed opposition movements against US funding for the conflict. High-profile figures like tech mogul Elon Musk and Fox News host Tucker Carlson called for his release, bringing global attention to his case. The news of Lira’s deteriorating health emerged from communications between his father, Gonzalo Lira Sr., and the US embassy. Documents and emails revealed attempts by Lira Sr. to alert the embassy about his son’s critical condition and the lack of transparency from Ukrainian authorities regarding his health status. “I cannot accept the way my son has died. He was tortured, extorted, incommunicado for 8 months and 11 days and the US Embassy did nothing to help my son,” Lira Sr. stated in an email announcing the news. “The responsibility of this tragedy is [with] the dictator Zelensky with the concurrence of a senile American President, Joe Biden,” he wrote, adding: “My pain is unbearable. The world must know what is going on in Ukraine with that inhuman dictator Zelensky.” In a poignant hand written note, Lira described his health ordeal, including double pneumonia, pneumothorax, and severe oedema. But whose definition of “propaganda” and “terrorism” are we talking about? When a state is accused of criminalising dissent, intimidating journalists, persecuting political opponents and targeting critics abroad, its demands for cooperation on online speech deserve exceptional scrutiny. Will British authorities distinguish genuine terrorist threats from peaceful political criticism? Will they safeguard UK-based journalists, dissidents and human rights defenders against politically motivated allegations originating from Pakistan? The UK must never allow legitimate counterterrorism cooperation to become a backdoor mechanism for surveillance, censorship or intimidation of people exercising their fundamental rights. Fighting terrorism is a legitimate responsibility. Silencing critics of those in power is not. And if Pakistan’s authorities want to discuss online propaganda, perhaps they should first explain why criticism of powerful generals is so often treated as a national security threat. Islamabad, London pledge deeper security cooperation Pakistan and the UK on Wednesday held their annual Counterterrorism (CT) dialogue, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. stories.text: Kokura was the miraculously spared original target for Fat Man, the USA’s second WW2 Japan nuclear bomb! There was low cloud cover and the USAF bomber had to choose a secondary target, Nagasaki. The Bombing of Nagasaki, August 9, 1945 Not only was the dropping of the second atomic bomb, after Hiroshima, when the Japanese wanted to surrender, immoral and unnecessary, we now know this was a Plutonium bomb which had been developed by the Nazis. Hiroshima’s ‘Little Boy’ was a much simpler Allied Uranium design. The US military had already successfully tried the Plutonium design on 16th July 1945, the ‘world first’, ‘Trinity’ test, at White Sands, New Mexico, but they wanted to glean the Plutonium a-bomb’s ‘kill metrics’ on a live target. The bombing of the Japanese city of Nagasaki with the ‘Fat Man’ plutonium bomb device on August 9, 1945, caused terrible human devastation. A B-29 named Bock’s Car took off from Tinian at 3:47 that morning. In its belly was Fat Man, and the atomic bomb was already armed. Major Charles W. Sweeney flew the plane while its namesake, Captain Fredrick C. Bock, piloted Sweeney’s usual mount christened “The Great Artiste.” The two men had switched aircraft as “The Great Artiste” held the sensitive measuring equipment used to monitor the atomic event. The Enola Gay took part in the mission, flying weather reconnaissance. Over Kokura, clouds and smoke from nearby bombing raids obscured visibility. The Americans could see parts of the city, but they could not sight directly on the city arsenal that was their target. Sweeney flew overhead until Japanese antiaircraft fire and fighters made things “a little hairy,” and it was obvious that sighting would be impossible. He then headed for his secondary target: Nagasaki. In Kokura, meanwhile, civilians who had taken shelter after the air raid signal heard the all-clear, emerged, and breathed sighs of relief. None of them knew then, of course, how close they had come to dying. Clouds also obscured visibility over Nagasaki, and Maj. Sweeney, running out of fuel, prepared to turn back toward Okinawa. At the last second a hole opened in the clouds, however, and Bombardier Capt. Kermit K. Beahan announced that he could see his target. And so Fat Man began its journey, detonating over Nagasaki at 11:02 a.m. local time. Fat Man detonated at an altitude of 1,650 feet over Nagasaki with a yield of 21 kilotons, about 40 percent more powerful than Little Boy had been. It did so almost directly above the Mitsubishi factories that were the city’s primary targets, rather than over the residential and business districts further south. Tens of thousands of civilians, especially children, had already been evacuated from the city. The series of hills bracing Nagasaki also somewhat confined the initial blast and restricted the damage.

stories.text: Surviving a nuclear bomb. Satellites and nuclear weapons in space. Golden Dome Is Technologically and Financially Infeasible For as long as nuclear-armed, intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles have existed, strategists and engineers have pursued a seductive idea: a shield effective enough to diminish — or even block — a ballistic missile attack. The appeal is obvious. A state that could reliably intercept ballistic missiles could protect its cities from these terrifying weapons and reduce its adversaries’ leverage. But defenses against strategic ballistic missiles have a long history of disappointments. Over roughly seven decades, the United States has spent more than $500 billion (in 2025 dollars) on missile defenses, much of it to defend against intercontinental ballistic missiles. And yet, the ability of any of these systems to intercept even a single missile or warhead under the conditions expected during a nuclear attack has not been demonstrated. Most recently, the Trump administration has proposed “Golden Dome” — an ambitious proposal for a comprehensive, layered defense with ground, sea, and space-based elements. It is supposed to protect the United States and its allies and deployed forces not only against attacks by ballistic missiles, but also by cruise missiles, hypersonic boost-glide vehicles, aircraft, and drones launched at any time from anywhere by any adversary, including peer adversaries. There is no prospect of deploying a missile defense system capable of successfully defending against a major ballistic missile attack by Russia and China for the foreseeable future. Such a system would have to be able to destroy hundreds or thousands of nuclear-armed long-range ballistic missiles or their warheads in the face of sophisticated countermeasures, dozens of decoys, and salvo tactics, as well as new delivery systems specifically designed to defeat it….

stories.title: Revolution or Extinction: the choice is ours – man made threats, can man unmake them.
stories.subtitle: World war. Revolution Or Extinction.
stories.text: Revolution or Extinction: the choice is ours – man made threats, can man unmake them. World war. Revolution Or Extinction. The Choice Is Ours. Humanity has the freedom to fail this test and go the way of the dinosaur. We’re allowed to take that path if that’s what we collectively choose to do. We can allow a few massively outnumbered plutocrats and empire managers to drive our species to extinction via climate disaster, nuclear holocaust, or AI apocalypse if we want to. We are completely free to do that. I don’t know about you, but I actually find this a comforting thought. When you take a close look at the existential hurdles that humanity is faced with, it can feel pretty bleak. Global capitalism is destroying the biosphere we all depend on for survival. The western empire is getting increasingly comfortable engaging in reckless brinkmanship with nuclear-armed rivals. The AI arms race is shoving through wildly unpredictable technologies at a rapidly accelerating rate with alarmingly little institutional oversight or caution. But when you notice that all of these existential threats are entirely man-made, you realize that this means humanity has the ability to un-make them as well. We have the freedom to do either. It’s up to us. I find this a comforting insight because it puts the ball in our court. We can choose to rise up and use the power of our numbers to save ourselves from doom, or we can choose not to. The universe, apparently, is fine with either choice. If it wasn’t, we wouldn’t be holding the ball. And who am I to argue with the universe? If the universe wants humanity to have the freedom to either go extinct in the near term or survive deep into the distant future, then I can make space within myself to allow that freedom, too. Whether or not we make it is not up to me as an individual. I can control my own actions, but I cannot control the actions of my fellow homo sapiens as a whole. And if our species as a collective decides that revolutionary change is not desirable enough or too scary or too difficult to seize, then I can submit to the will of the collective. I can hold enough grace and compassion for my species to honor its sovereign decision. “We’ll either pass the test or we won’t.” That’s what I tell myself when things are looking dark. I give humanity the freedom to make its decision, and in so doing I free myself. I do what I can to move the needle in whatever way my limited means allow me to, and then beyond that I submit to the will of our better angels. I do my work, and then I let go. I let go and enjoy my time on this beautiful blue planet here. Because I don’t know how much longer it will last.

stories.text: Algorithms and search engines. Marginalia. What Marginalia is, and why the verdict is an own index Marginalia is a search engine built by one person in Sweden that crawls the web itself and ranks it more or less backwards from the way Google does. Heavy JavaScript, dense advertising, affiliate links, tracking scripts and modern optimized design push a page down. What rises instead is text: personal sites, old blogs, university department pages, hobbyist documentation — the parts of the web with no marketing budget and consequently no visibility in mainstream results. Marginalia runs its own crawler, stores its own index (the engine’s stored copy of the web), applies its own ranking, and involves no Google or Bing feed anywhere. Its FAQ states flatly that the engine does its own crawling — and unusually, that claim can be checked from outside rather than taken on trust. The project’s framing is more modest than the coverage around it. It is not seeking to replace Google and Bing, it says, but to complement them — to provide a minority report that keeps them honest. It is a discovery instrument, not a general-purpose answer engine, and has never pretended otherwise. The FAQ gives roughly 300 million documents as of 2024, occupying about a terabyte, and that page flags itself as outdated; the current about-site says only “hundreds of millions of documents.” No dated 2025 or 2026 figure exists, so none is asserted here. Against Google’s trillions this is four to five orders of magnitude smaller, and the project treats that as a design position rather than a shortfall. The FAQ’s own formulation is the clearest sentence about the whole project: an index with a million documents that are all of high quality is better than an index with a billion documents where only a fraction are interesting. Marginalia is principally developed and operated by Viktor Löfgren, a Swedish software engineer, working essentially alone. No company, no board, no investor. Wikipedia records maintenance at around an hour a week. The about page gives operating costs of approximately $200 a month and describes the project as running on donations, grants and commercial API deals, with no investor pressure — designed, in its own words, to scrape by. There is no advertising and none planned. The commercial leg is a keyed API: SearXNG’s Marginalia module, for instance, requires a key issued under Marginalia’s own license terms. There are also no AI features, deliberately — no AI answers, no chat, no LLM summarisation. The project positions against the trend, holding that traditional information-retrieval approaches still offer capabilities that have largely become lost. It is a keyword engine by conviction, for users who want to steer a query rather than ask a question. The inverse is quietly true: because it offers a clean keyed API over an index of non-commercial text, it has become attractive to people building AI and research tooling. Marginalia does not do AI; AI systems increasingly want Marginalia.

Tommy Robinson found guilty of harassing Daily Mail journalists after jurors heard he used ‘bully-boy tactics’ to intimidate reporters who exposed his UK riots shame Tommy Robinson has been convicted of ‘weaponising social media’ to harass two Daily Mail journalists who exposed him stoking race riots in the UK from his sunbed in Cyprus. The former English Defence League leader was convicted by jurors after they heard he used ‘bully-boy, intimidatory tactics’ to threaten the reporters. The political activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, sent photographers to their addresses and shared images of their homes with millions of social media followers, prosecutors said. Journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber described how they ‘feared for their safety’ after Robinson, 43, sent a series of posts and direct messages on social media platform X. The court heard Robinson sent Mr Dirnhuber a message saying, ‘I’ll be knocking on your door,’ and when a photo was posted on X of Mr Dirnhuber outside his home, wrote: ‘Got ya.’ Jurors heard he also phoned Mr Young to tell him: ‘I’m coming to get you.’ Robinson denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence and said the journalists would have known he was not ‘coming to beat them up’. But Robinson faces a possible jail term of up to ten years after he was convicted by jurors today at Southwark Crown Court. He showed little reaction as the verdicts were returned. Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counter terrorism division, said Robinson ‘weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence’. Speaking following the guilty verdicts, he said: ‘The evidence in this case showed that he targeted the victims directly and indirectly through social media and by telephone. He also published images relating not only to them, but also their families. ‘The jury heard from the victims and witnesses in this case, ultimately deciding that this behaviour crossed the line into criminality. Prosecutor Ben Holt told jurors how Robinson targeted the journalists after the Mail published a front-page story about him in August 2024. ‘The jury heard from the victims and witnesses in this case, ultimately deciding that this behaviour crossed the line into criminality. The Met said anyone behaving as Robinson did ‘to intimidate, harass and threaten others either online or in the real world can expect to be investigated and brought before the courts’ ‘Nobody should be made to fear violence because of the work they do. Journalists play an important role in a democratic society and should be able to carry out their professional duties without being subjected to harassment. ‘We will always seek to work with the police to prosecute those who break the law and I hope these convictions provide reassurance that such behaviour will be treated seriously by the criminal justice system.’ The story had the headline ‘Stoking race riots from his sunbed’ and was based on unrest in the UK sparked by the murder of three girls in Southport. Mr Holt said Robinson could have complained to Ipso, the independent Press regulator, about the exclusive article. Instead, he ‘retaliated’, warning: ‘You have come for me, I am going to come for you.’ Mr Holt told jurors: ‘This defendant, using bully-boy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. ‘The journalists feared for their own personal safety and also for their own family, either being forced to leave home or employ security personnel to watch their home.’ Robinson told police the Daily Mail had identified his hotel in Cyprus and he was ‘overrun with news crews taking photos and filming my children’, who were ‘scared and upset’. Mr Holt said: ‘His case is that his family had been put in danger by the actions of the Daily Mail.’ However, no identifiable pictures of his children were published by the Daily Mail. Reporter Mr Dirnhuber was left ‘scared to go to my own house’ in the wake of Robinson’s social media messages, while freelance journalist Mr Young said he felt his family was under threat because of the harassment by Robinson. Mr Dirnhuber said he feared being ‘intercepted’ by a supporter of Robinson on his way to work, who may have been ‘hoping to cause me or my partner physical harm’. He said he and his partner decided to leave their home until security provisions had been put in place – including a doorbell camera and assessing the feasibility of a panic alarm.
