stories.text: BBC QT – Is Burnham playing with fire reigniting Brexit debate? Burnham reignites Britain’s divisive Brexit debate with his push for closer EU ties LONDON (AP) – For a decade, British governments have observed a cardinal rule: Don´t mention Brexit. In particular, don´t suggest that voters´ 2016 decision to leave the European Union should be reversed. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who marked his 100th day in office on Tuesday, has broken that code of silence and reignited a debate that bitterly divided the country. He says Brexit has been a failure and the U.K. should seek a much closer relationship with the EU, with options up to and including rejoining the 27-nation bloc. “I am positive about closer ties with Europe and I´m not hiding that,” Burnham told the Sunday Times. “I think it will add to British GDP. I think it will give us stronger control of migration. I want to make those arguments.” In recent interviews, Burnham has said the country should have an “evidence-based debate” about the consequences of Brexit. He gave the example of immigration. Supporters of Brexit argued that it would give the country control over its borders by ending the right of EU citizens to live and work in the U.K., and of British nationals to settle across the bloc. While Britain now sets its own immigration policy, Burnham said leaving the bloc had made it harder to control unauthorized migration because Britain has lost access to EU databases and agreements. “The truth of the matter is we´ve lost immigration control in the way that we once had,” Burnham told broadcaster ITV on Monday. Some economists think that Brexit has hurt the British economy, but few politicians have wanted to reopen the painful debate. The decision of British voters, by 52% to 48%, to leave the bloc after four decades of membership was followed by years of U.K.-EU wrangling over divorce terms. Britain finally left the EU in 2020 with a bare-bones trade deal that erected new barriers to doing business with the bloc of 450 million people on the U.K.´s doorstep. In seeking closer ties, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc´s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers. Burnham says that could change after the next national election, which must be held by 2029. He told the Labour Party´s annual conference last month that “Brexit has done more harm than good” and he will seek political consensus on a new relationship, with future options including rejoining the bloc. A U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on Nov. 20 is set to discuss a more limited reset: a trade deal for food and drink, agreements on energy and emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU…

The Greater Manchester mayor, who is expected to challenge Sir Keir Starmer for the Labour leadership if he wins the Makerfield by-election, said Brexit had been “damaging” but “Britain will be stuck in a permanent rut if we’re just constantly arguing”. He has already been cleared to seek selection as Labour’s candidate, after the current MP Josh Simons stood down to make way for him, although he still needs to be chosen by the local party. In a speech at a conference in Leeds, Burnham said: “My view is that Brexit has been damaging, but I also believe the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments.” He added: “I am not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU. “I respect the decision that was made at the referendum and it is going to undermine everything I have said about strengthening democracy if we don’t respect that vote.” Sir Keir has already been seeking closer ties with the bloc, but has stuck to Labour’s election manifesto pledges to “stay outside the EU”, with “no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement”.

How Zionist terrorism determined Palestine’s fate Israel’s propaganda playbook attempts to reframe the Palestinian liberation struggle as a question of terror, not territory . Thanks to a dutiful media, this effort to portray Palestinians as terrorists has had significant traction among some demographics. But how did terrorism originate in Palestine and what was its outcome, both historically and today? Thomas Suárez sheds much new light on those questions in State of Terror: How Terrorism Created Modern Israel. He does this largely by mining previously neglected declassified documents from the British National Archives, covering the period of the British Mandate for Palestine (1920-1948). Suárez’s principal thesis is that Zionist terrorism “ultimately dictated the course of events during the Mandate, and it is Israeli state terrorism that continues to dictate events today.” The author cautions that while he unequivocally condemns Palestinian terrorism against civilians, he recognizes that some were driven to extreme measures due to an asymmetry in power and in reaction to attempts to subjugate the Palestinian people and expropriate their resources, land and labor. Zionist terrorism aimed to prevent Palestinian Arabs from exercising their right to self-determination, Suárez argues, and when an aggressor encounters resistance, it can hardly use self-defense as a justification for its own acts of violence. “Otherwise,” Suárez writes, “all aggression would self-justify.” Suárez is not a professional historian. However, State of Terror has drawn praise from such figures as Israeli historian Ilan Pappe who – on the book cover – calls it a “tour de force” and “the first comprehensive and structured analysis” of the violence employed by the Zionist movement both before and after Israel’s creation. Indeed, Suárez’s scholarship is impressive and the book includes nearly 700 endnotes consisting mainly of original sources.

Private enterprise is corroding and penetrating the fabric of the NHS at every level’ Allyson Pollock, Clinical Professor of Public Health at Newcastle University,US health care, is taking shape in the UK Professor Allyson Pollock wrote in her 2006 book: NHS plc: The Privatisation of Our Healthcare, that: “The permeation of NHS management and hospitals and health authority boards by business is emblematic of the way in which private enterprise is penetrating and corroding the fabric of the NHS at every level. ” Given the recent disclosure by the news group Belfast Live that revealed a dramatic increase in the amount of public money being channelled to private healthcare providers across Northern Ireland since 2020. In the five financial years between April 2020 and April 2025, the combined total spend on private healthcare appointments by the Health and Social Care Trusts in Northern Ireland totalled at least £302,203,303, I was keen to get Professor Pollock’s views on this. “Northern Ireland and England have gone down the same route of outsourcing, largely elective surgery and diagnostics. So that’s NHS-funded care in the private sector, whereas Scotland decided, after a bit of an abortive start in 2003, to actually reverse the decision to privatise and outsource. It’s actually continued to try and build capacity in its own NHS. “So while, of course, you do increase capacity, what happens is that the private sector ends up cherry-picking because they can’t provide the same level of services the NHS, they can’t provide intensive care units and intensive care beds. So they cherry pick the healthier and wealthier patients and leave the poor ones behind in the NHS. “But overall, waiting times have been rising for everybody, Inequalities are rising because the capacity in the NHS to treat is shrinking. “There’s fewer beds being used for elective surgery so people who are poorer and less healthy are waiting longer. “That’s quite shocking. There’s another issue here, which is readmissions. So readmissions are very common after hip and knee surgery and cataract surgery, but it’s about five per cent of all admissions are readmitted. stories.text: CAN ANYONE PLEASE FIND AND UPLOAD THIS DOCUMENTARY? A Prescription for Murder? Panorama Is it possible that a pill prescribed by your doctor can turn you into a killer? Over 40 million prescriptions for SSRI anti-depressants were handed out by doctors last year in the UK. Panorama reveals the devastating side effects on a tiny minority that can lead to psychosis, violence, possibly even murder. With exclusive access to psychiatric reports, court footage and drug company data, reporter Shelley Jofre investigates the mass killings at the 2012 midnight premiere of a Batman movie in Aurora, Colorado. Twenty-four-year-old PhD student James Holmes, who had no record of violence or gun ownership, murdered 12 and injured 70. Did the SSRI anti-depressant he had been prescribed play a part in the killings? Panorama has uncovered other cases of murder and extreme violence which could be linked to psychosis developed after the taking of SSRIs – including a father who strangled his 11-year-old son. Panorama asks if enough is known about this rare side effect, and if doctors are unwittingly prescribing what could be a prescription for murder.

stories.text: RAF Bomber Command 1939 to 1945 documentary – with Dr Robin Clifton of Warwick University. Len Deighton book on history of WW2. Blood, Tears and Folly: An Objective Look at World War II is a 1993 book by Len Deighton is a history of World War II from an alternative viewpoint. Deighton looks for the origins of the war, from the rise of the great power conflicts that led to the First World War, through the inter-war years and the histories of the various conflicts and combatants in the years up until the beginning of the war in 1939. He traces the early engagements, the feints, the so-called Phoney War, right through until Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941. Deighton attempts to create an encyclopedic introduction to the conflict by building up a detailed background and showing how perilous Britain’s early situation was, the early blunders by Winston Churchill in the Norwegian Campaign and the British dealings with the French that led to the debacle of Dunkirk. Deighton, a skilled thriller writer, does an exemplary job here of deconstructing the strategy and stupidity of WWII from the British POV. A comparable American-centric work is the ‘Army at Dawn’ trilogy. Nations start wars, and their generals plan battles, often based on wishful thinking instead of facts. When confronted by disaster, they often double-down. As the Allies turn the tide and defeat the Nazis, it is often startling that any success could be achieved. This is the epiphany that Deighton’s work sparks. “Blood, Tears and Folly” is, like Deighton’s other notable non-fiction, about warfare, and the Second World War in particular (with some “setting of the scene” going back thirty or more years in European or world history). His central thesis is that, despite the best efforts of some historians, the actual story of the war in its initial stages is one in which the Allies (the Brits in particular) were overconfident in their ability to respond to the German threat, and in turn doomed themselves to being overrun by the Blitzkrieg of early 1940. No one comes off well here, as Deighton seems to take down many of the mythic figures on the Allied side who have since been revered for their military strength or national importance. This includes Churchill, by the way, and coming from Deighton (as British a writer as you’ll ever find), that says a lot. Do I agree with all of Len’s arguments here? Not necessarily, but I find his writing style entertaining, even when discussing horrible things. And there was a lot of horror during the war, from the obvious widespread murder of the Holocaust and Japanese atrocities in China and elsewhere to the less obvious ones. Deighton can be cranky at times, and I don’t dispute his anger at some of the mistakes as he sees them that unfolded. Overall, I think it’s always best to approach any work of narrative history with a healthy skepticism about the author’s ability to tell the story without leaving something out or being guilty of shaping the tale to fit a narrative. So with that caveat in mind, I think it’s fair to suggest this book as a handy one-volume rundown of some of the war’s less heroic moments, with the understanding that it’s all one man’s perspective. Len Deighton was a wonderful writer, whose fiction has come to mean a lot to me as the last few years have gone by. And this book, which I first attempted to read as a weird teenager during the years when the world seemed to finally be at peace, is a helpful reminder that on the world stage, people fuck it up pretty handily from time to time. The Second World War was a global conflict that didn’t have to happen, if Hitler had been more forcefully opposed and if the Allies hadn’t been more wary of Communism than Fascism. And it could have ended a lot sooner if those same governments had taken the threats seriously or responded more promptly to battlefield outcomes. It really was a war that changed the world, and in “Blood, Folly and Tears,” Len Deighton proves that it was a war that exacted a heavy price for sins of omission and commission on near equal terms.

[ download pdf ] In her 1944 book ‘Seed Of Chaos’ Christian WWI nurse and writer Vera Brittain warns against RAF Bomber Command’s ‘decent into barbarity’ which she says is laying the foundations for a future Third World War. ‘Among the majority at any rate, the desire for revenge and a hardening process – even If, for a time, it may be subdued by fear? Thus we are steadily creating in Europe the psychological foundations for a Third World War. Fourthly, the systematic destruction of German industrial power is hItting ourselves from a long-term standpoint. The prosperity of the Continent in the past has largely depended upon German industry, and the continental market, including Germany, was the best block of markets for the British export trade before the War. Mr Harcourt Johnstone, Secretary of the Department of Overseas Trade, said on 4th November, 1943, that in order to maintain our standard of lIfe after .the War, we should need to increase our export trade by £350 million a year ‘. The destruction of German industry means the destruction of the biggest British export market, and makes it more dIfficult, if not impossible, to prevent the lowering of the standard of life m Great Britain for many years after the War. !he second main argument brought forward to excuse our present policy of obliteration bombing is that we too have suffered – as indeed we have – and that therefore we are fully entitled to pay back what we have endured. . Mr George Bemard Shaw has dealt characteristically and drastically WIth this double contention in a recent letter to the Sunday Express (November 28th, 1943): !he blitzing of the cities has carried war this time to such a climax of infernal atrocity that all recriminations on that score are ridiculous. The Germans will have as big a bill of atrocities against us as we against them If we take them into an impartial international court. there are three further replies which should also be carefully considered by all rational people. In the first place, investigations into the origins of civilian bombing far from the fighting lines (as distinct from the bombing which forms part of a military campaign) make clear the difficulty of justly assessing. wIth who~ lays the fault of starting it. The cumulative growth of ciIvlian bombmg to Its present nightmare stage seems, on present inforrmatlon, to be an outstanding instance of the tragic fashion in which war-time cruelty grows like a snowball by its own momentum once the power of Juggernaut has taken control. Some accidental violatIon of international law, assumed to be deliberate, is repaid by a reprisal in kind . The enemy ‘hits back’; we retaliate harder still; in each case the accidental consequences (such as the bombing of a church in mistake for a factory) are advertised for propaganda purposes by the victim as having been intentional. So the grim competition goes on, until the mass-murder of civilians becomes part of our policy – a descent into barbarism which we should have contemplated with horror in 1939. Secondly, it is a fact – as this book will show – that though parts of Britain suffered cruelly in the Blitz, some of the terrible inventions and tactics now being used were not known or practised at that stage of the War. Even in those early days, the knowledge of our distress and confusion was limited to the areas which endured them, and particularly to the surviving victims and to Civil Defence and rescue workers, who had actually to deal with the shambles to which German bombs reduced many humble homes. It is, I believe, the comparative rarity of first-hand experience among the majority of the British people which accounts for their supine acquiescence of obliteration bombing as a policy.’ My own experience is relatively small, but as a Londoner who has been through about 600 raid periods and has spent 18 months as a volunteer fireguard, I have seen and heard enough to know that I at least must vehemently protest when this obscenity of terror and mutilation is inflicted upon the helpless civilians of another country.’

stories.text: Slaughterhouse 5 novel about the RAF bombing of Dresden. Slaughterhouse-Five, or, The Children’s Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death is a 1969 semi-autobiographic science fiction-infused anti-war novel by Kurt Vonnegut. It follows the life experiences of Billy Pilgrim, from his early years, to his time as an American soldier and chaplain’s assistant during World War II, to the post-war years. Throughout the novel, Billy frequently travels back and forth through time. The protagonist deals with a temporal crisis as a result of his post-war psychological trauma. The text centers on Billy’s capture by the German Army and his survival of the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war, an experience that Vonnegut endured as an American serviceman. The work has been called an example of “unmatched moral clarity” and “one of the most enduring anti-war novels of all time”. The book has been translated into at least 11 other languages, including German (twice), Italian (twice), French, Polish, Portuguese, Bulgarian, and Chinese. The novel’s first chapter begins with “All this happened, more or less”; this introduction implies that an unreliable narrator tells the story. Vonnegut utilizes a non-linear, non-chronological description of events to reflect Billy Pilgrim’s psychological state. Events become clear through flashbacks and descriptions of time travel experiences. In the first chapter, the narrator describes his writing of the book, his experiences as a University of Chicago anthropology student and a Chicago City News Bureau correspondent, his research on the Children’s Crusade and the history of Dresden, and his visit to Cold War–era Europe with his wartime friend Bernard V. O’Hare. In the second chapter, Vonnegut introduces Billy Pilgrim, an American man from the fictional town of Ilium, New York. Billy believes that an extraterrestrial species from the planet Tralfamadore held him captive in an alien zoo and that he has experienced time travel.

stories.text: BBC 4 Extra – Great Lives – Shirley Williams on her Mum, Vera Brittain. Vera Brittain Great Lives The writer and pacifist Vera Brittain is discussed by her daughter Baroness Shirley Williams and Dr Clare Gerada, Chair of the Royal College of GPs. Vera Brittain’s life was shaped by the grief that followed the loss of her fiance, her brother and two good friends. She candidly conveyed the toll of the First World War on her generation in the best-selling 1933 book, Testament of Youth. Matthew Parris chairs an insightful exploration of what it was like to be brought up by Vera a mother who was, for many reasons, simply unavailable to the young Shirley Williams. Vera was a teenage feminist desperate for an education. But she turned her back on her studies at Oxford in 1914 because she felt compelled to serve as a nurse, wanting to join her brother and his friends in the trenches. Shirley Williams explains that as a result of her experiences, Vera became a committed pacifist, at a time when it was deeply unpopular to do so. Dr Clare Gerada nominates a fascinating life while paying tribute to two women – mother and daughter – who she believes have made the 21st century a better place for women to live. Produced by Mark Smalley. First broadcast on BBC Radio 4 in 2012.

The King and Queen arrived at the Senedd to loud chants of “not my King” and “down, down, down with the Crown”. Protesters waiting outside the Senedd held placards which read “abolish monarchy” and “down with the crown”, while there were also signs showing Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and the late Virginia Giuffre. The chanting could be heard clearly as the royals walked up the Senedd steps to greet First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth and Huw Irranca-Davies, the Llywydd (presiding officer). Protesters held a placard with an image of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (Image: Ben Clinton / Republic) The protest was organised by anti-monarchy group Republic, and marks the first demonstration against the royals since a court ruled on the legality of search warrants used during Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest in February. Republic have called for the investigation into the disgraced former royal to continue and for a full enquiry to be held into what other members of the royal family knew and when. Republic CEO Graham Smith commented: “Charles shouldn’t be rocking up to the Senedd, Scottish Parliament or the House of Commons. He’s an unelected head of state who should have no place in our political institutions. “Andrew is trying to obstruct the police investigation into serious allegations. Charles clearly has questions to answer about what he knew about these allegations and for how long.” Protesters gathered outside the Senedd for the arrival of the King and Queen (Image: Ben Clinton / Republic) Smith continued: “Andrew has been accused of various offences for years. For years the police, government and the royals turned a blind eye to protect him from scrutiny.” “Republic’s position remains clear – police must follow the evidence wherever it leads and continue their investigation.” Smith said that “Wales doesn’t need a prince” and “Britain doesn’t need a king”. “What we need are answers to some straightforward questions and justice for victims of serious crimes,” he continued. He was expected to say that the funding – known as the sovereign grant – must be revised as Britain endures a lasting cost of living crisis. And on this week’s episode of the Mirror’s award-winning podcast Pod Save the King, the cash for the monarch is discussed and it is questioned if theere should be more transparency on royal finances. Russell told the YouTube show: “How can you sort of sit back and have a man at the top of the shop [King] who is worth £2 billion, and we are still paying for the fuel for their helicopter and for the royal train to leave the station? I think that is a bitter pill to swallow for a lot of people.” The Mirror’s deputy royal editor Jennifer Newton agreed, as she argued that if the monarchy was more forthcoming with their finances, the public would be able to have a more informed opinion about how taxpayer cash is being used. Jennifer explained: “I think if there was more transparency, even if the numbers don’t look particularly good or the optics aren’t good, but at least if they were being a bit more transparent, we could then have a more honest conversation and debate about it.” Russell agreed, saying: “It is a fine balancing act. I understand where Lord is coming from, but it will be very interesting to see if this gains any traction. Because, I mean, I think we are in such a state, not only here but across the world, of this cost of living crisis that is just unending. The £100 million Sovereign Grant covers expenses for the royal’s engagements(Image: WPA Pool, Getty Images) “And how on earth can we keep on funnelling this money? Should the government be putting more pressure, rather than sort of treating the royal family with kid gloves? Are we getting value for money?” Lord Foulkes previously told the Mirror he was incensed by the monarch’s use of private jets and helicopters and questioned why the family needs so many homes while making public statements on homelessness. He was expected to tell peers that the UK has by far the most expensive state-funded monarchy in Europe as he argued the Sovereign Grant is too high. The former Scotland Secretary was to say in his address: “When we ask the public to fund an institution to the tune of over just under £100 million a year through the Sovereign Grant, at a time when many are facing severe pressure on their household budgets, we have a duty to ask two fundamental questions – are we getting value for money, and do the actions of this institution match the values it preaches? I would argue that the answer to both is no.” Lord Foulkes added: “While European neighbours have streamlined their royal houses, we continue to fund a sprawling network of ‘working royals’ whose ribbon-cutting duties would, in any other sector, face strict audit and productivity metrics.” The grant is an annual payment to fund the monarch’s official duties, such as overseas and domestic trips, while also paying for the ongoing £369 million refurbishment of Buckingham Palace. The payment – based on profits from both the Crown Estate and taxpayer funds – also covers the cost of employing staff, upkeep on royal residences around the UK, and hosting official events such as garden parties and state visits. stories.text: Richard Kay – Mountbatten stopped relationship with John Spencer and Queen. Why Earl Spencer’s damning memoir rings so true to me… They last met at London’s Tate Gallery on July 1 – Princess Diana’s 36th birthday. It was unexpected. ‘Neither of us had any idea that the other was going to be at the evening,’ Charles Spencer observed. Typically, he noted, his sister was not celebrating her special day with friends but was working: guest of honour at a charity fundraiser. They were never to see each other again. Nine weeks later, with Diana dead and a nation convulsed in grief, Earl Spencer was to recall this briefest of final encounters in his powerful eulogy from the pulpit of Westminster Abbey. From time to time Earl Spencer, the baby brother whom Diana had mothered as a child, would speak out against some of the more lurid fantasies. Occasionally he would take aim at the royals too: one year complaining that William and Harry may not have been encouraged to stay in touch with their mother’s side of the family; another, wondering why the then Prince Charles had never visited his ex-wife’s island grave at Althorp, the Spencer family home in Northamptonshire. But mostly he kept quiet, as he and his family tried to hold fast to their memories of the woman to whom he paid such moving tribute. Now, with the 30th anniversary of the princess’s death 11 months away, comes, at last, Charles Spencer’s own brilliant examination of his sister, in order to right some of those wrongs. It is an explosive yet thoughtful book, simply entitled Swan Song. But it is at times unflinching when it comes to Diana in the raw, the sister he so memorably described from the Abbey pulpit as ‘a very British girl who transcended nationality’. It is an insider’s account from the ultimate insider, one of only a handful who knew Diana for almost the entire span of her life. It is elegiac and moving, with childhood memories of growing up with Diana, who was three years his senior. But it is also at times painful, as the rollercoaster of the princess’s life escalated to a whirlwind pace on marrying the heir to the throne. Nor does he shrink from how her celebrity impacted his family – the fallings out and the breakdown in relations. At the time of her death, she had not spoken to their mother for almost four months. And he details his own quarrel with her, when he changed his mind about allowing Diana the use of a property she had her heart set on at the Althorp estate. But for King Charles the memoir is a catastrophe. All his careful efforts to rebuild the affection of a nation that was repelled by his treatment of Diana but has come round in the years since – especially since he assumed the crown – risk being brutally stripped away.

Mossad interventions in UK. Last March, top national security officials gathered inside the White House to discuss with Mr. Trump how to respond to the nerve agent attack in Britain on Sergei V. Skripal, the former Russian intelligence agent. London was pushing for the White House to expel dozens of suspected Russian operatives, but Mr. Trump was skeptical. He had initially written off the poisoning as part of legitimate spy games, distasteful but within the bounds of espionage. Some officials said they thought that Mr. Trump, who has frequently criticized “rats” and other turncoats, had some sympathy for the Russian government’s going after someone viewed as a traitor. During the discussion, Ms. Haspel, then deputy C.I.A. director, turned toward Mr. Trump. She outlined possible responses in a quiet but firm voice, then leaned forward and told the president that the “strong option” was to expel 60 diplomats. To persuade Mr. Trump, according to people briefed on the conversation, officials including Ms. Haspel also tried to show him that Mr. Skripal and his daughter were not the only victims of Russia’s attack. Ms. Haspel showed pictures the British government had supplied her of young children hospitalized after being sickened by the Novichok nerve agent that poisoned the Skripals. She then showed a photograph of ducks that British officials said were inadvertently killed by the sloppy work of the Russian operatives. Ms Haspel was not the first to use emotional images to appeal to the president, but pairing it with her hard-nosed realism proved effective: Mr. Trump fixated on the pictures of the sickened children and the dead ducks. At the end of the briefing, he embraced the strong option. The outcome was an example, officials said, of how Ms. Haspel is one of the few people who can get Mr. Trump to shift position based on new information. “Her style and the way she projects herself in these kind of senior situations is disarming, without showing weakness,” said Doug Wise, a former C.I.A. officer who has worked with Ms. Haspel.

The Greens Look To Get Serious On The Economy Green Party figures are wrestling with a question: how can they demonstrate economic credibility while maintaining their radical edge? It was a talking point at their conference in Brighton over the weekend. Harriet Lamb, Green Party CEO, told a fringe event hosted by More in Common that looking “competent on the economy” would be important to the party’s next steps as it tries to build on the growth it has achieved since Zack Polanski took over as leader. At the same event, the think tank’s executive director, Luke Tryl, presented data showing that the public views a Green Party focus on the economy almost just as favourably as a focus on the environment. Among a section of avid Green supporters, which More in Common calls Progressive Activists, a focus on the economy is significantly more popular. Senior Green figures who PoliticsHome spoke to in Brighton said the party must prepare for intense media scrutiny of its economic policies in the months ahead – particularly if there is talk of the role the party could play in a coalition government. To that end, the Greens are planning to expand their team of economic spokespeople, with councillors elected in May in the pool of people being considered, PoliticsHome understands. The Secretary of the Greens’ Economy Policy Working Group, Nadine Storey, admitted there is some nervousness within the party about presenting a different economic approach to the Westminster orthodoxy as “you need spokespeople who can defend the policy”. Speaking to PoliticsHome in Brighton, she said: “Zack has been very good at that. “He’s been much bolder, braver at being prepared to take on the journalists, but he has been caught out once or twice because he didn’t know the nitty-gritty.” On Sunday, Green conference voted in favour of a motion setting out what Storey described as “underpinnings” to the party’s radical economic policy. It includes dropping interest rates as the main means of controlling inflation; no longer using Gross Domestic Product as a measure of economic policy success; and abolishing the Office for Budget Responsibility. Party rules mean that the motion is now official policy.

Chris Busby on the death of Petra Kelly, German Green Party, and her husband, just before their documentary on real effects of Chernobyl to be made. The Green Party and Nuclear Energy Christopher Busby The recent Brighton conference policy change of the Green Party of England and Wales to embrace nuclear energy was sad but not unexpected. I have believed since Fukushima that the nuclear operators (which we used to call the nuclear military complex, or their agents, the nuclearists) had started seriously focusing on the last political fortress of those opposing nuclear. In the hysteria following Fukushima, they were forced to bring out their Queen, George Monbiot and his Guardian megaphone. This began with his Pauline conversion (no one has died from the radioactive releases) and moving to his attacks on me, on Christopher Busby (false scientist, fraud). I have written and spoken elsewhere that all that he said about me (peddling anti-radiation pills and making stupid epidemiological mistakes) was a pack of lies and half-truths, supported by bogus scientists like Gerry Thomas so I won’t say any more here about that. Except that the Green Party immediately disowned me, and all the funding I was receiving (Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust, the Goldsmiths, the Gillettes) vanished. But at the time, I was the Green Party National Speaker on Science and Technology, and immediately following Fukushima, I explained the problem on prime-time TV News for the BBC and also ITN. You can see these interviews on Youtube still. Everything I said then (opposed by some pro-nuclear furby) has since been shown to be true. Cancer and leukemia rates have increased in Japan, and also generally every country that provides cancer data. But the Green Party began as an anti-nuclear party in Germany, with Petra Kelly. When I chained myself to the gates of Trawsfynydd Nuclear Power Station in Wales in 1992, Petra Kelly had agreed to come and support our campaign against opening the nuclear site, which was dangerous. The station operators had applied to run the reactors at a high temperature to anneal the cracks in the pressure vessel. This was not long after the experiment at Chernobyl. And the contamination of Wales by Chernobyl (which led to sharp increases in cancer and child leukemia). The Aftermath: The protest successfully amplified the public safety debate surrounding the station’s embrittled reactor pressure vessels. It is frequently cited by Busby and Green Party organizers as a pivotal moment of non-violent pressure that ultimately pushed the operator to announce the plant’s permanent economic closure the following year. We were all a bit scared by this project. The nuclear police had pistols and we were told they would shoot us. Petra Kelly was assassinated a few months after this. How can I say this? How do I know? Well, of course I don’t know and cannot be sure. But here is something you don’t know about this. The story now widely accepted (look at Wikipedia) is that her man, General Gert Bastiaan killed her. The police determined that Kelly was shot dead while sleeping by Bastian, who then died of suicide. Well and Good. But I spoke with Prof Ernest Sternglass about this. He knew both of them, and said it was impossible that Bastiaan would have killed her and himself. They were full of positive energy and life, when he met them in Berlin some 6 weeks before she died. She was very excited. She had received an offer of considerable financial support by German TV to make a series of documentaries with Russian and Belarussian scientists including Dr. Shevchenko, to report on the real health effects of the Chernobyl accident contamination. At the time, the nuclear operators and their tame scientists in the IAEA and the WHO were stating that there were no measurable health effects. It was the same at Fukushima some twenty years later. But back in those days they killed you, rather than using media to destroy your credibility. Erin Brockovitch for example. Ernest told me he later had a phone call from Shevchenko from Mexico who told him he was on the run and feared for his life.

Green Party vote for policy on mass UK job creation and reining in the financial banksters: The first and most fundamental duty of a civilised state is the safety of its people. Not just safety from overseas adversaries, or crime in the street. Economic security. A bill you can pay without going overdrawn. A house you can afford before your children have children of their own. A job that lasts long enough to plan around. Britain guarantees none of these. Not for want of money, or land, or people who know how to build. Our nation has all of that. For forty years we have outsourced that security to the global marketplace. We locked ourselves in a room and posted the key to a trading desk in New York. British government policy subservient to global winds. They call it living within our means. We call it Hostage Nation. Renationalisation. Hostage Nation is about escaping four words: ‘we can’t afford it’. Four words that have stunted our nation’s ambition, destroyed communities and damaged our collective pride. Most people want climate action, lower bills, decent jobs, and affordable homes, and they want to see a plan to deliver it. We’ve looked under the bonnet of the economy; the money is there, the powers are there, but the political bravery is missing. The government is in a unique position to rebuild Britain where privatisation has failed, with the health and security of the British people as the bottom line. If we continue to allow volatile international bond markets to dictate whether we build railways or schools, we are hostage to the whims of foreign trading floors. If our only response to global energy prices is to hike mortgage rates and business lending, then we are just compounding our citizens’ misery. If every £1 spent on retrofitting a house saves the NHS 40p, perhaps there’s another way. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country. This is a plan that protects the people of Britain from the next inevitable economic shock. Jamie Driscoll is a Green Party Councillor in Newcastle and the former North of Tyne Mayor. During his time as Mayor he created 5,377 jobs, 2,133 homes, ran projects in 240 schools, including child poverty prevention. He also negotiated a £6.1bn devolution deal with the then Tory government. He was blocked by the Labour Party in 2023 from standing as North East Mayor, a decision that drew criticism from many in the party, including Andy Burnham and Steve Rotheram. He ran an independent campaign which secured 126,652 votes, the second-highest number of votes for an independent candidate in UK political history. Biochar Pioneer – Ed Revill Ed Revill lives in South Gower, where he implements the theories of soil carbon regeneration on his market garden. He runs workshops on using appropriate technologies, including biochar stoves. “Biochar is charcoal intended to be used as a soil additive rather than to be burnt. There are two main reasons for making and using it: firstly, to improve crop yields by increasing the soil’s nutrient holding capabilities, increasing moisture retention, reducing acidity and influencing the activity of the soil micro organisms; and secondly, to stabilise the carbon in biomass and thereby sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide.” Permaculture People UK Swansea Biochar – Ed Revill Behind an enormous pile of wood chip lies Ed Revill’s market garden. On a scorching summer’s day we passed healthy looking rows of potatoes, wheat and alliums to cross a field towards a collection of semi hidden structures behind a small, yet productive forest garden. We found Ed picking leaves in his prolific polytunnel. Known as ‘Biochar Ed’ to many, Ed greeted us with his characteristic humility and enthusiasm. A repository of vast amounts of knowledge Ed speaks with an ardent urgency evidenced in the multiple tracks of thoughts that rush out of his brilliant mind. We were soon introduced to one of his inventions – a biochar rocket stove. We had encountered biochar during our time in Costa Rica so it was interesting to see its application in a more familiar setting. Carbon negative cup of tea anyone? Ed’s enthusiasm for biochar is perhaps best explained by the man himself, who, in a three part series for Permaculture Magazine, discusses the creation, and application, of biochar – including his own biochar rocket stove hybrid. “Biochar is charcoal intended to be used as a soil additive rather than to be burnt. There are two main reasons for making and using it: firstly, to improve crop yields by increasing the soil’s nutrient holding capabilities, increasing moisture retention, reducing acidity and influencing the activity of the soil micro organisms; and secondly, to stabilise the carbon in biomass and thereby sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide.” The TLUD stove, where we made all our tea and cooked all our meals (we scratched together handfuls of plentiful woodchip from the nearby polytunnel floor), was a cinch to use. Over the sound of a whirring fan and hum of the brilliant smokeless flame, Ed took us through the mechanics of his outdoor stove. Inspired by the work of Paul Anderson and his work on biochar stoves Ed created his own version which he had recently designed and got working. Made of two chambers in a reused gas cylinder, woodchip is deposited into the inner chamber: a container for a loose bulk material that tapers downward and is able to discharge its contents at the bottom. Air, with the assistance of a battery powered fan, is drawn in as the woodchip is lit from above. Most of the air goes up between the two cylinders and is blown through a ring of holes. The wood gases rise and you get a ring of fire at the top. Because there is not enough air in the retort (the outer chamber) for the combustion of the wood chip, pyrolysis occurs. Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) – A failure ?by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a ?food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday. The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran. “It’s absolutely crucial to ‘get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season,” he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of ?the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings. In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military ?has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait. “The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran’s attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait ?of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage,” he said. The White House and Iran’s Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Iran has sought to tighten ?its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports. Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world’s most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies. Fertilizer ?shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note ?last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a “very negligible” share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said. The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify ?cargo loading. The passage of only five vessels ?per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer ?supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said. Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added. MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through ?intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran’s conditions and ?Washington’s insistence on addressing ?Iran’s nuclear programme from the outset.

stories.text: South African Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize – Chair of UN Commission that called Gaza genocide. Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize Pillay was told of the award in Nuremberg’s Palace of Justice Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The South African judge was recognised “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, which paved the way for a “more comprehensive global legal order”, the Nobel committee said. Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza. Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country’s fifth Peace Prize winner – following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Pillay’s work had been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted”, said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” he said. “At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity.” Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, “so my message to her would be ‘if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'”. Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg’s Palace of Justice by saying “it must be a joke” and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her. “If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” she joked. Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as “recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom”. Pillay dedicated her award to “all the survivors of international crimes” and the practitioners of international justice “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign”. Navanethem “Navi” Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver’s daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban. She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country’s high court. Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda – focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed – including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2003…

Green Party abandons opposition to nuclear power A major shift in policy The Green Party has voted through a new policy on electricity generation which abandons the its blanket opposition to nuclear power. Party members voted for a motion at the party’s conference which amended the party’s policy so as to describe nuclear fission as a form of ‘low-carbon electricity generation’. It also removed nuclear power from the list of electricity generation sources that the Green Party would seek to ‘phase out’. Instead, the party says it now only seeks to phase out fossil fuels. The Green Party has long opposed nuclear power, instead favouring an approach to decarbonisation which relies on a rapid and overwhelming shift to renewable energy. The party’s previous policy stated “Other industries can never be sustainable and must be phased out, for example, the nuclear industry.” That wording has been changed, so it now refers to fossil fuels instead of nuclear.

stories.text: ITV News – Gloucester Docks silted up as Bristol Water extracts too much water after dry summer. Privatised Bristol Water shareholder oligarchs sucking out the pure water – leaving the silt in dock and canal – Will £4m dredging solve a dock’s silt problem? The £4m dredging project to remove silt from a city’s docks has begun, but what is the long-term solution to prevent it from returning? Silt levels at Gloucester Docks became so high this summer that water depths fell below navigable levels, leaving boats trapped and forcing the docks to close. The Canal & River Trust (CRT), which manages the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, began dredging on Monday, with the work costing the trust about half of its total dredging budget. But Gloucester MP Alex McIntyre said this was only a short-term solution, adding: “We are going to keep seeing this problem as climate change gets worse.” The silt has become visible in Gloucester Docks in recent weeks, forcing it close What is causing the silt? Silt typically enters Gloucester Docks because water has to be pumped from the River Severn into the canal to keep it functioning. During long periods of dry weather, lower river levels can mean water is drawn from areas closer to the riverbed, where the concentration of sediment is often higher. This can result in more silt entering the system. There has also been speculation that the build-up of silt has been made worse due to water being pumped from the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal to supply drinking water to people in Bristol. There has been a long-term agreement since the 1960s to supply water to Bristol from the canal. This has led to some to question if Bristol Water stopped this process, would CRT not need to pump as much water, and therefore silt, from the River Severn?

stories.text: Green Party vote for policy on mass UK job creation and reining in the financial banksters: The first and most fundamental duty of a civilised state is the safety of its people. Not just safety from overseas adversaries, or crime in the street. Economic security. A bill you can pay without going overdrawn. A house you can afford before your children have children of their own. A job that lasts long enough to plan around. Britain guarantees none of these. Not for want of money, or land, or people who know how to build. Our nation has all of that. For forty years we have outsourced that security to the global marketplace. We locked ourselves in a room and posted the key to a trading desk in New York. British government policy subservient to global winds. They call it living within our means. We call it Hostage Nation. Renationalisation. Hostage Nation is about escaping four words: ‘we can’t afford it’. Four words that have stunted our nation’s ambition, destroyed communities and damaged our collective pride. Most people want climate action, lower bills, decent jobs, and affordable homes, and they want to see a plan to deliver it. We’ve looked under the bonnet of the economy; the money is there, the powers are there, but the political bravery is missing. The government is in a unique position to rebuild Britain where privatisation has failed, with the health and security of the British people as the bottom line. If we continue to allow volatile international bond markets to dictate whether we build railways or schools, we are hostage to the whims of foreign trading floors. If our only response to global energy prices is to hike mortgage rates and business lending, then we are just compounding our citizens’ misery. If every £1 spent on retrofitting a house saves the NHS 40p, perhaps there’s another way. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country. This is a plan that protects the people of Britain from the next inevitable economic shock. Jamie Driscoll is a Green Party Councillor in Newcastle and the former North of Tyne Mayor. During his time as Mayor he created 5,377 jobs, 2,133 homes, ran projects in 240 schools, including child poverty prevention. He also negotiated a £6.1bn devolution deal with the then Tory government. He was blocked by the Labour Party in 2023 from standing as North East Mayor, a decision that drew criticism from many in the party, including Andy Burnham and Steve Rotheram. He ran an independent campaign which secured 126,652 votes, the second-highest number of votes for an independent candidate in UK political history. In 2024, he founded Majority, a grassroots organisation focussed on developing the competent and compassionate leaders needed on the progressive left. Hugo Fearnley is a long-time political adviser to Jamie Driscoll, having first worked together at the North of Tyne Combined Authority. He is a former Research Fellow at Northumbria University and previously led press and communications at public ownership campaign group We Own It. Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg is a British politician and broadcaster who served as a Conservative Member of Parliament from 2010 to 2024. A prominent advocate for Brexit, he held senior government roles including Leader of the House of Commons and Business Secretary. stories.text: Cost of living crisis – how to get outgoings down. Typical family £2,900 worse off due to cost of living crisis, think tank finds Report: Five years of a near-continuous cost of living pressures have caused the real incomes to fall by almost 8% The cost of living squeeze has wiped almost 8% off an average family’s possible income, says report(Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto) A typical family is £2,900 worse off this year because of the continuing cost of living crisis, a think tank found. New analysis published by the Resolution Foundation discovered the past five years of a near-continuous cost of living pressures have caused real incomes to drop by almost 8%. The report assesses the toll of three crises – the aftermath of the Covid crisis, the invasion of Ukraine, and conflict in the Middle East – during which inflation peaked at 11.1%. It says energy has been at the “epicentre” of a price shock for households. Higher energy costs have bled into other prices, with food inflation peaking at nearly 20% in March 2023. The pain felt from these price rises has not been shared equally, the think tank found. Inflation was steepest for essentials, which make up a larger share of poorer households’ spending. As a result, the rise in non-housing costs since before the pandemic has been around one-sixth bigger for the poorest tenth of households than for the richest tenth, the report concluded. Overall, it says that the real income of a typical working-age household this year is £2,900 a year lower than they would have been compared to a world in which inflation had stayed at 2% over the past five years. Energy have been one of the biggest blows to households since 2021 TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak said: “Household budgets have been hammered by the consequences of Donald Trump’s and Vladimir Putin’s reckless warmongering. “The government must use this month’s Budget to deliver the circuit breaker the Prime Minister has recognised the country needs “Working people shouldn’t be left to carry the cost while banks pocket billions from higher interest rates. After five years of profiting from global turmoil it’s time the banks paid their fair share and helped shield families from soaring bills.”

stories.text: Journalist Ian Proud , aka Peacemonger, detained at airport on return from Valdai conference in Russia – why has West given up on diplomacy with Russia – diplomacy is compromise. Why war with Russia is inevitable. It may be a European extinction event. The Peacemonger I will join a panel at the Valdai discussion club today on the title of Europe of the future: before the war or after the war. I make the case that the UK has been at war with Russia since 2014 and that the EU finally joined the war in 2022. That is on the basis that foreign policy consists of three components. The first, espionage, will always happen in war or in peacetime. even between allies . We all spy on each other. The other two core component are diplomacy and warfare. The UK chose not to pursue diplomacy in June 2014 and therefore chose war. Initially that consisted of economic warfare through sanctions. Then it chose to support proxy warfare in Ukraine itself. It is in January 2022 that Europe final set itself on war, upon the death of the Minsk 2 agreement. Right now, both the UK and Europe continue to refuse diplomacy and therefore are pursuing a system of war. It’s important to understand that the whole system of government is locked into the war mentality. The Prime Minister, ministers, parliamentarians, most of them, the mainstream media, the think tank circuit by and large. Choosing diplomacy is now impossible because that would require a whole of system shift. Even if the Prime Minister tried to pursue diplomacy the rest of the system would resist, especially the mainstream media, but also officials, many parliamentarians, some Ministers and think tanks. So the system is locked on a war mentality. It is important to understand this. The only way the system can reset to diplomacy is either if the west inflicts a strategic defeat on Russia, which continues to look highly unlikely. Or if the material conditions in Ukraine and Europe become so bad that the system decides it has no choice to shift to a diplomacy footing. Despite the suffering in Ukraine and the grinding economic fragmentation and decline of Europe, there is little evidence of the system wanting to reset to diplomacy as, to do so, would be to recognise that the material conditions of the Ukraine war had turned against them. They would have to admit defeat to a public they have been trying to convince since 2022 in total victory over Russia since 2022. That makes the choice of full general war with Russia now almost inevitable unless there is a radical political shift across Europe which appears unlikely. We are rolling the dice in the hope that a general war doesn’t lead to nuclear escalation on the basis that we cannot bear to admit defeat in Ukraine. Everyone should be deeply concerned about this and lobby their governments for peace and diplomacy. Without that, I fear, many of us will die because of the folly of our political elites.
